opus-5.5.text:
So I think the thing people consistently get wrong is they pick the false-positive rate based on what looks good in a paper rather than on what a human on the other end of the alert can actually tolerate. You'll see someone say, "Our detector has a 1% false-positive rate," and that sounds great in a table. But then you ask: how many events does this thing see per day? If it's scanning a million requests, that's ten thousand false alarms a day. Nobody is going to look at ten thousand alerts. They're going to look at the first fifty, find that forty-nine of them are nonsense, and then they're going to mute the channel. And at that point your detector has an effective true-positive rate of zero, because nobody's listening.

So the way I like to think about it is to start from the human budget and work backwards. How many alerts per day can the person or team responding realistically investigate with real care? Maybe it's five. Maybe it's twenty. Then you divide by the volume of traffic, and that tells you the false-positive rate you actually need. Very often that number is something like one in a million, or one in ten million, which is many orders of magnitude below where most research papers report their operating points. And this is why I'm always asking people to report true-positive rate at very low false-positive rates, rather than accuracy or AUC, because AUC averages over a whole bunch of regions of the curve that nobody would ever deploy at.

The other piece is base rates. If the thing you're trying to catch is genuinely rare, say one actual attack in a million events, then even a detector with a one-in-a-million false-positive rate means half of your alerts are false. People really underestimate how brutal that is. Precision is what the human experiences, not the false-positive rate, and precision depends enormously on how rare the real thing is.

And then there's a dynamic element that I think matters a lot. Trust in an alerting system is something you build up and spend down. If the first several alerts someone sees are real, they'll take the next one seriously even if it's a little ambiguous. If the first several are garbage, you've lost them, and it's very hard to win them back. So in practice I'd much rather ship something that's extremely conservative, that fires rarely but is almost always right, and then gradually loosen the threshold as people gain confidence in it, than ship something that catches everything and gets ignored.

Last thing I'd say, especially in an adversarial setting: the false-positive rate you measure on your test set isn't necessarily the one you'll see in deployment. Distributions shift, benign users do weird things you didn't anticipate, and if there's an adversary, they're actively trying to push their stuff to look benign while you might also have people pushing benign things to look malicious, just to flood you. So you want margin. Whatever number you calculated from the human budget, I'd aim meaningfully below it, because reality is almost always going to be noisier than your evaluation.

r001.rationale: The response says genuine alerts build trust and garbage alerts undermine it, but does not say that occasional false alarms about human presence can increase confidence that a camera will detect a real person.

r002.rationale: It explains that too many false alarms lead people to mute the alert channel, so they stop paying attention to warnings.

fable-5.1.text:
So the thing I always come back to is base rates, because that's where almost everyone's intuition breaks. People will say, "my detector has a one percent false-positive rate, that's great." And one percent sounds tiny until you remember that the thing you're trying to catch is almost never happening. If you're looking at, say, a million queries a day and the actual attack rate is one in a hundred thousand, then a one percent false-positive rate means ten thousand false alarms for every ten real events. Nobody is going to look at the ten real ones. They're buried. Your detector is, in practice, worthless, even though on paper it looks fine.

So I don't think about false-positive rate as a number I pick in isolation. I think about it as: how many alerts can a human actually tolerate before they start ignoring the system? That's the real constraint. Humans habituate incredibly fast. If an analyst sees twenty alerts a day and nineteen of them are nothing, by the end of the week they're clicking dismiss without reading. At that point you've built something that is actively worse than nothing, because now you have a false sense of coverage.

The way I'd frame it is you work backwards. You figure out the volume of traffic, you figure out the realistic rate of the bad thing, you figure out how many investigations a person can do carefully, and then that tells you what false-positive rate you need. And very often the answer is something like one in a million, or one in ten million, which is a number people find absurd when they first hear it. But that's just the arithmetic.

And the uncomfortable part is that at those rates, you usually can't even measure the false-positive rate well. You don't have ten million clean examples lying around that you've verified. So you end up having to be a little humble about what you actually know, and you design around it. You layer things. You use a cheap, noisy detector to narrow a million down to a thousand, and then a more expensive, more careful one to narrow that to ten, and then a human looks at ten. Each stage can have a mediocre false-positive rate on its own as long as the whole pipeline ends up somewhere a person can actually engage with.

The other thing I'd say is that the cost of a false positive isn't uniform. If the action on detection is "log it and move on," you can tolerate a lot. If the action is "lock the account" or "block the user," then every false positive is a real person having a bad day, and you need to be far more conservative. So the question "what false-positive rate" is really "what false-positive rate given what happens next," and I think people skip that second half far too often.

r001.rationale: The response discusses base rates, alert volume, and false-positive costs, but does not convey that occasional false alarms about human presence can increase confidence in a camera’s ability to detect a real person.

r002.rationale: It says repeated unimportant alerts make analysts start dismissing alerts without reading, so important ones can be ignored.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to start with the base rate: how often is the thing you’re trying to detect actually happening? And then ask what somebody is supposed to do when the detector fires.

Suppose you’re looking at a million things, and only ten of them are actually malicious. A false-positive rate of one in a thousand sounds pretty good. But that gives you about a thousand false alarms and, at best, ten real ones. If a person has to investigate each alert, you’ve built a system where almost every time it asks for their attention, it’s wrong. They’re going to stop paying attention, quite reasonably.

So I would work backward from the operational constraint. How many alerts can someone investigate? How costly is an investigation? How bad is it to miss something? That tells you what part of the detector’s performance curve matters. You might prefer a detector that catches fewer attacks but produces alerts you can actually act on. The goal isn’t just to detect things; it’s to make the person using the system more effective.

r001.rationale: The response discusses false alarms and alert fatigue generally, but does not say that occasional false alarms about human presence can increase confidence in a camera’s detection of a real person.

r002.rationale: It says that when almost every alert is wrong, users will stop paying attention, conveying that excessive unimportant warnings can lead users to disregard important ones.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to start with the base rate. How often is the thing you’re trying to detect actually happening? Because a false-positive rate that sounds very low can still mean that most of your alerts are wrong.

Suppose you’re looking at a million things, and only a hundred of them are malicious. If your false-positive rate is one in a thousand, you’ll get about a thousand false alarms. Even if you catch every malicious example, most of what you flag is benign. And the person looking at those alerts is going to learn pretty quickly that they can ignore them.

So I would work backward from what happens when you raise an alert. Who has to investigate it? How much time does that take? What happens if you’re wrong? Then choose a threshold that makes the alerts useful within that workflow. Sometimes that means accepting that you’ll miss more attacks in exchange for having a system whose warnings people actually act on.

r001.rationale: The response discusses false alarms generally, but does not convey the cited paper’s argument about occasional human-presence alarms increasing confidence in camera detection.

r002.rationale: It says that when most alerts are false, users learn to ignore them, including alerts that may matter.
